On the first Saturday of June, the town of Marlow holds its annual river festival. Volunteers arrive before seven to set up stalls along the towpath, and the smell of frying onions drifts over the water by mid-morning. Children queue for the rowing boats while a brass band plays on the green. The organisers have run the event for thirty-two years, and each summer they publish a small booklet listing the stallholders, the times of the races, and the names of the volunteers who have helped since the beginning. The festival began in 1992 as a small gathering of neighbours and has grown into the busiest weekend of the year.

This year the booklet is longer than usual. A new path has been laid from the car park to the bandstand, and the council has planted a row of lime trees along its edge. The old wooden bridge, closed since the spring, reopened in May after repairs to its stone footings. Residents say the bridge makes the walk from the eastern side of town much shorter, and the cafe by the lock has been busier ever since.

The festival committee met on Thursday evening to review the arrangements. They discussed parking, the position of the first-aid tent, and the timetable for the raft race. Someone raised a question about the noise from the stage after ten o'clock, and the chair promised to speak with the band. A separate meeting will be held next month to decide how the stalls are allocated. The treasurer read out the notes from the previous year, and everyone agreed that the arrangements had worked well.

On the day itself the weather was kind. Families spread blankets on the grass and shared sandwiches while the children ran between the stalls. The mayor opened the proceedings with a short speech, thanking the volunteers and the local businesses that had helped with the arrangements. A display of old photographs in the village hall drew a steady stream of visitors, many of whom stayed to talk about the houses they had lived in as children.

By late afternoon the queue for the boat rides stretched past the bandstand. The organizers counted more visitors than in any previous year, and the cake stall sold out before four o'clock. Two of the volunteers, who had been at every festival since 1994, were presented with a small engraved plate. A few visitors mentioned the length of the queue, but most simply waited in the sunshine.

The mayor, speaking at the close of the afternoon, said the new library had already changed the town. Children who once waited for a bus now walk there after school, and the reading room stays open until eight on weekdays. "The greatest benefit of the whole project," she said, "is that it belongs to everyone."
